How other harnesses are built

The course teaches one machine. These are four real ones, and what each is worth reading for. The point is not to copy them; it is to see the same seams at different scales.

ProjectLanguageSizeRead it for
piTypeScriptabout 11 packagesthe complete event and extension model
PiGGoa line-by-line port of pithe same design in Go, with parity tests
crushGoabout 49 internal packageswhat Go wants to look like at scale
fxZig719k lines, 667 filesthe smallest concept count that still works

pi

The reference implementation of everything this course teaches, plus the parts it deliberately skips: extensions, a tree-shaped session, compaction as a session entry, thirty provider adapters, and a terminal UI.

Read these files in order.

FileWhat it shows
packages/agent/src/agent-loop.tsthe loop: stream, buffer calls, run them, append results, repeat
packages/agent/src/types.tsthe event union, and the before/after tool hooks
packages/ai/src/api/openai-completions.tsthe provider client you wrote in chapter 01, with retries and caching
packages/mcp/a hand-rolled MCP client over stdio
docs/how-pi-works.mdthe architecture in prose, without code

PiG

pi rebuilt in Go as one binary, with a parity harness that runs the same scenario against both implementations and diffs the results.

Read it when you want to see the course's architecture in the language you are writing. Two things are worth more than the code: test/parity/ is a working example of a harness that tests a harness, and docs/parity/PORT_MAP.md shows how to keep a port honest.

crush

The most idiomatic Go harness. Its loop is not in the repository at all: it comes from charm.land/fantasy, which makes crush an adapter around a shared loop. That is worth knowing before you go looking for loop.go.

Read it for structure rather than for the loop.

PackageWhat it shows
internal/permission/a permission service, rather than a hook
internal/agent/coordination, tool dispatch, queueing
internal/mcp/MCP through the official Go SDK
internal/lsp/what a real editor integration costs
internal/ui/a Bubble Tea interface over agent events

fx

The minimal end of the spectrum, and the best evidence for the claim that a harness is a library with injected capabilities rather than an application.

The marketing says 6.66 MiB. That number is a macOS arm64 build. Linux x86_64 is 13.39 MiB, and the source is larger than crush. What is genuinely smaller is the concept count: a host supplies instructions, tools, network, storage and permissions, and the core does the rest.

One measurement from it is worth carrying into your own work: a cold request was 23,884 bytes, and 15,560 of those were tool schemas. Sixty-five percent of a request was definitions, before any conversation existed. That is why chapter 07 counts both budgets.

What the four agree on

  • One call, one result. A tool call resolves exactly once, including on failure.
  • Results keep source order. Execution order is yours; append order is not.
  • The model is behind a seam. Every one of them can be pointed at a different

provider without touching the loop.

  • Context is the scarce resource. They differ in how they bound it, not in

whether they do.

What they do that this course does not

Extensions and plugins, a terminal UI beyond a chapter list, editor integration, image input, provider authentication, background subagents, and evaluation harnesses. Where next lists which of those is worth building on top of what you have, and which is a different project.
